rows.why: The 14-day expiry and the unused starting state are fixed requirements. The only open question here is what happens when a new code collides with an existing one, and that is item 8. Its pick redraws the code, which matches the scenario.
No item asks this. Item 12 is about the order of a contributor's task list and duplicates in it, not whether redeeming grants access to just that task and records who used the code and when.
Item 4 asks whether codes are matched exactly or leniently. Its pick uppercases the code and strips whitespace and dashes, so lowercase, spaced or dashed input is read as the same code.
Item 2 asks about the exact 14-day boundary. Its pick treats now >= createdAt + 14 days as expired, so a redeem at 08:59:59.999 works and one at exactly 09:00:00 fails with "expired".

No item asks what happens when the same contributor redeems their own used code again. Item 1 covers redeeming a different code for a task the contributor already has, which is S7. Item 5 is about which reason wins between used, revoked and expired, which this scenario doesn't involve.

Item 6 asks whether codes can be revoked and what revoking a used or unknown code does. Its pick adds revoke and throws on used codes, which matches "a used code cannot be revoked". A revoked code being refused follows from having revoke at all. Item 11 covers only the "unknown" reason, so item 6 is closer.
Item 1 asks exactly this. Its pick returns "already has access" and leaves the code unused.

Item 7 asks how simultaneous redemptions are handled. Its pick runs registry operations one at a time through a shared queue, so only one redeem wins even when the store resolves late. The other fails with "used".

Item 9 asks what list returns. Its pick gives each code's state at the current time but doesn't say which fields are shown, such as who used a code and when. It also doesn't say whether a used code stays "used" after its expiry time, so there's no way to tell if it matches.
